topic: Unlocking Discrete Convolutions: From Image Blurring to Feature Extraction
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Computer Science or Engineering

sections.title: Introduction: The Concept of a Moving Window (1 min)
sections.content: Define discrete convolution as a mathematical operation on two functions, focusing on the 'sliding window' approach. Introduce the two components: the Input Signal (the map) and the Kernel/Filter (the lens).
sections.example: Imagine a flashlight (the kernel) scanning over a pitch-black room (the signal) to reveal specific objects one by one.

sections.title: The Mechanics: Weighted Summation (1.5 mins)
sections.content: Explain the step-by-step process: overlay, multiply element-wise, and sum. Emphasize how the kernel 'weights' neighboring pixels. Use a 3x3 grid animation to show how a center pixel value changes based on its neighbors.
sections.example: A cat walking on a grid of numbered tiles; the cat's influence (kernel) is strongest on the tile it stands on and fades towards the adjacent ones.

sections.title: Prerequisite Visual Intuition: Kernels as Filters (1 min)
sections.content: Briefly review the prerequisite that a kernel is a matrix of numbers. Explain that changing these numbers changes the 'intent' of the convolution: smoothing (blurring) vs. sharpening (edge detection).
sections.example: Using a 'Blur' filter like a fogged-up window versus an 'Edge Detection' filter like a high-contrast ink sketch of a rabbit.

sections.title: Real-World Applications: AI & Beyond (1.5 mins)
sections.content: Connect the theory to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Explain how multiple layers of convolutions allow a device to 'see' abstract features like shapes, then textures, and finally objects.
sections.example: A smart camera on a delivery drone: early layers detect lines, middle layers detect shapes like wheels, and final layers identify the delivery box.
